Introducing 𝚡𝚎𝚎𝚝: https://t.co/YaLEMbmKwf.

A hermetic, pixel-perfect X post renderer in safe Rust / wasm. Zero browser,
items.content:
Introducing 𝚡𝚎𝚎𝚝: https://t.co/YaLEMbmKwf.

A hermetic, pixel-perfect X post renderer in safe Rust / wasm. Zero browser, network, filesystem, system fonts. Renders a post to PNG in ~1ms (and 0.4 ms for @jack's "setting up my twttr" 😁).

X is the global town square, and the medium is the message. Being able to preview what things will look like before posting is great for both humans and agents.

Rendering with xeet is is 100x-1000x faster than booting up a browser and taking a screenshot, yet it's just as accurate.

It reproduces Blink & HarfBuzz text shaping, 1/64px line breaking, RTL bidi, 28 Chirp font subsets, CJK/Math/Emoji fallbacks, "Show more" rules, etc. It's the kind of thing that would be wildly impractical, if not impossible, for a human engineer to pull off.

Except 𝚡𝚎𝚎𝚝 is structured as an "autorepo." An oracle boots up Chrome, and verifies tens of thousands of text layout rules. A CI canary then watches the evolution of the original, and files signed PRs for agents to act on. It was conceived from the ground up around 'verification engineering', and the result speaks for itself.

Enjoy!

items.title: In democratic societies, everyone has *some* responsibility on how the use of  technology maximizes benefits and minimiz
items.content:
In democratic societies, everyone has *some* responsibility on how the use of  technology maximizes benefits and minimizes bad side effects. 
The benefits of AI are real today, and will greatly expand in the future. 
The bad side effects have, so far, been minimal. 
It's on all of us to make sure it remains that way.

The catastrophe scenarios (extinction, employment apocalypse, etc) are totally ridiculous for anyone who understands how thing work in the real world.
And the p(doom) estimates are all pulled out of their authors' back ends. It makes no sense to attribute a probability to events over which we have complete agency. Whatever probability you come up with merely reveals your lack of confidence that your fellow humans will do the right thing. Confidence in humanity is one thing Geoff and I disagree on.
The other thing we disagree on is the primacy of intelligence. In the real world, intelligence is not synonymous with power and dominance. A virus, a poisonous snake, or a tiger can bring down a human. Lots of very stupid humans dominate much smarter ones (just look at the international political scene). 

Superintelligent AI will work for us and do our bidding, subject to safety guardrails.
It will have no desire to take over.

I have made detailed technical proposals for AI architectures that can be made safe by satisfying safety guardrails at inference time.
I call it Objective-Driven AI Architecture.

items.title: I think the explosion of “neolabs” in quantitative trading has been brought about by a misconception either in the compe
items.content:
I think the explosion of “neolabs” in quantitative trading has been brought about by a misconception either in the competitive landscape OR where money is made in quantitative trading.

The idea that a startup claims to be the first to pursue “the bitter lesson” in quantitative trading is absolutely ludicrous. 

Top tier quant funds have long been hiring AI researchers and training end-to-end (industry parlance: tick-to-trade) models for years. From memory: HRT, UbiQuant, XTX, HighFlyer (hello, deepseek?!), and many, many, many more.

In every podshop, there is at least 1 team with a focus on creating large scale end-to-end models that “train on markets directly”.

If you CLAIM to be the first, you either don’t understand the landscape or are straight up lying, or don’t even have the slightest clue on the SOTA problems being worked on by your past employers.

—

I can’t speak to their skills, but there is some insinuation here that training the largest model and throwing a lot of data at the model will “solve” quantitative trading.

Markets are for better or worse, reflexive. That makes it hard for anyone to achieve high predictive power for a long time. Research is almost always a constant race to maintain your position - unlike more general machine learning, there is no evidence that SoTA models in markets have been able to continuously improve their predictive power beyond a certain threshold.

The implication here is that money is often made not purely from the models, but also the non-trivial technological and operational scaffold of being able to monetise low signal-to-noise models.

Spoken plainly, there is a lot of work to be done across the entire investment process in order for a single dollar to be generated. 

When one has been a fledgling researcher, he is tasked only to focus on and think about the model. And upon any initial success, he is almost always convinced that his portion is the lion’s share of the work, oblivious to the thousand moving parts that made his model work.

items.content:
Don't use Claude until you read this: 

(then send it to your entire team)

> first, switch this on (nothing works without it)
> settings → capabilities → "Create and edit files"
> on Enterprise? your admin has to turn each tool
> Go to organization settings → then artifacts
> on Free plan: you still get Docs, Slides & Design
> everything you make gets stored in the Artifacts tab (left sidebar)

CLAUDE MOTION (the animated video one)

> never let Claude invent your facts. Instead
> attach the report, your logo, your screenshots
> add this line to every prompt:
"One idea per scene. Max 8 words on screen."
> if it's for Reels? ask for vertical, 1080 × 1920
> the music is muted by default. click the speaker
> To have it more polished. open it in Adobe, Descript or Runway

CLAUDE DATA (it was called Dashboards)

> it needs a live connection to your data
> if you want only a CSV, use Claude Sheets instead
> start with this prompt:

"I need to decide [the decision]. Put the 3 numbers that matter most at the top, each compared with last month. Then show me why: break them down by [channel / team / region]. Tell me every assumption you made."

> then change it by asking: "Add a filter for region."
> your data team can certify a query
> the chart then gets a "certified" badge

CLAUDE SHEETS

> every cell gets outlined, in case Claude corrects it
> for wrong edit? click on version history to restore
> limit: 100,000 cells per sheet. no pivot tables
> read-only on your phone
> a sheet can't feed a dashboard (yet)

CLAUDE WHITEBOARDS 

> drag a box around one area > ask about that part
> Claude only reads what's on the board, not apps
> so paste your context on the board first
> "follow" a teammate to see what they see
> when done, send it to Miro or export a PNG

CLAUDE MEETINGS

> owner: organization settings → products → Claude Meetings
> auto-join: settings → capabilities → Meetings
> pick "all meetings" or "all except one-on-ones"
> to not interrupt, type your ask in the Meet chat
> it keeps the transcript, not the audio
> notes & transcripts are free during the beta
> a week later, ask in any chat: "what did we decide about pricing?"

BONUS: chain them

> on a whiteboard: "turn this board into a deck"
> in Data: ask for a short narrated video of your dashboard
> and Claude Design closes on December 14
> move your projects into the Artifacts tab before that

I built an open-source library on GitHub to remake any website. And no, I still don't know how to code.

Go to Awwwards to find award-winning websites.

Go to OnePageLove .com for single-page websites

It keeps your website’s code.

4. Now, create a free Vercel account.

It publishes your website on the internet.

5. Go to the Claude desktop app → Code.

Pick a new, empty folder on your desktop.
Select 'Auto' mode & Opus 5.5 on High.

6. Paste the prompt & replace the link with the website you picked.

"/goal Remake [THE WEBSITE URL YOU CHOSE] with github .com/rubenhassid1/remake until its report says REMAKE COMPLETE, or stop after 100 turns."

9. The last step has to be: Make it yours.

Replace the inspiration website text with yours.

A brief history of AI Coding since Nov 2025:

Nov 2025: Opus 4.5 releases, OpenClaw gets built
Dec 2025: community agrees that models get good enough to handle 95% of coding tasks
Jan 2026: Ralph loops get popular, early efforts on loops/orchestration
Feb: Everyone feels knackered, too much strategic decision-making, fears around cognitive debt begin
Mar: Skills explosion as community converges around easy-to-share processes (superpowers already ahead of the game here)
Apr: most SOTA devs haven't written a line of code in months
May: "The unreasonable effectiveness of HTML" - more interest in richer review surfaces
Jun: "Loop Engineering" wins vaguepost of the year, signals more hype around process
Jul: Every talk in every conference becomes "here is my software factory"
Aug: Opus 5 speaks incomprehensibly, interest in ASD-STE100 peaks
Sep: Grok Bot gets popular, more interest in long-running "manager" threads which retain context and delegate work
Oct: The promised speed gains haven't materialised, "dark factory" feels a long way off still
Nov: No-slop manifesto releases, reading the code still appears essential

TL;DR: no-one is writing code anymore, and we are still figuring out what that means

items.content:
how to test your aws app for free

with aws's new local emulator no aws account needed

the play: install the emulator > point your cli or sdk at it > run your tests > deploy to real aws once it works

> fastest way: let your coding agent set it up

- update the aws cli to 2.35.0 or later
- run: aws agent-toolkit add-skill --skill-name aws-emulator --region us-east-1
- ask your agent to set up the emulator

> manual setup

- linux: install the rpm or debian package, run aws-emulator
- mac / windows: run it in docker from the short dockerfile in the docs
- set the env vars to point your sdk at the emulator
- run your code as usual

> how normal people can use this

you don’t need to be a pro

- students / beginners: practice s3, dynamodb, sqs, lambda etc. without creating an account or risking a surprise bill
- hobbyists & side project builders: prototype your whole app locally, break things freely, then deploy only when it works
- teachers / workshop runners: demo aws services without forcing everyone to sign up or share credentials
- anyone with a coding agent (cursor, claude code, kiro, etc.): just tell the agent “set up the aws emulator and build x”. it handles the rest

it keeps everything in memory on your machine. restart the emulator and the slate is clean. no real resources, no real money spent

> why ai builders care

- your agent can create and break resources without touching your real aws account
- it runs in cli, so your tests never call aws

> what not to do

- don't use it for production
- don't use it to test security
- don't assume every api works, check the things that do not work

> the catch

- some aws apis don't work yet, the repo tracks them
- telemetry is on by default. turn it off: aws-emulator --telemetry off
- building from source needs 100gb+ of disk, use the prebuilt package

advice: give your coding agent the emulator first. let it break things locally, then deploy

One "fix this bug" run is luck. LoopForge turns your team's delivery method into SOPs that coding agents can loop-run in the cloud:

→ Roles, not vibes. Plan / code / review / test are separate agents. The writer isn’t the reviewer.

→ Script gates + human sign-off. Builds and tests decide by exit code, not an agent’s word. Nothing ships without approval.

→ Engineering-grade RSI. Each run is scored 0–100; the replay surfaces what broke and writes improvement prescriptions back into SOPs, roles and gates — you review, then apply.

→ Bring your own agents. 10 swappable CLIs (CodeBuddy, Codex, Claude Code, Cursor…). MIT, self-hosted, your keys and code stay on your infra.

Code was never the bottleneck. The handoff is — and LoopForge catches the baton.
